cards.title: Flying squirrels glow bubblegum pink under ultraviolet light
cards.body: In 2019, researchers accidentally discovered that North American flying squirrels emit a bright bubblegum-pink glow under ultraviolet light. Biologists tested museum specimens dating back a century alongside wild squirrels, finding that all three native species fluoresce. While glowing fur is common in marine animals, it is extraordinarily rare in mammals. Scientists suspect the fluorescence aids nighttime navigation through snowy forests or helps squirrels communicate in the dark.

sources.title: Flying squirrels glow pink under ultraviolet light

cards.title: George Washington's famous false teeth were never made of wood
cards.body: Despite popular legend, George Washington never wore wooden dentures. His dental prostheses were actually crafted from carved hippopotamus and elephant ivory, cow teeth, brass screws, and genuine human teeth—some likely purchased from enslaved workers at Mount Vernon. Because porous ivory stained easily from wine and food, Washington's dentures quickly took on a yellowish-brown, grained hue. This discolored, aged appearance likely convinced observers that the first president was chewing with carved timber.

cards.title: The machine that invented cotton candy was patented by a dentist
cards.body: In 1897, dentist William J. Morrison teamed up with candy maker John C. Wharton to invent the world's first electric spun-sugar machine. Marketed as "Fairy Floss," the confection melted crystalline sugar and spun it through tiny holes using centrifugal force. The duo introduced the treat at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, selling over 68,000 wooden boxes. Morrison later served as president of the Tennessee State Dental Association.

sources.title: Fairy Floss, Cotton Candy, and Dentists

cards.title: Owls cannot roll their eyes because their eyeballs are actually tubes
cards.body: Unlike humans, owls cannot move or roll their eyes to look around. Their eyes are elongated tubes rather than spheres, held rigidly in place by bony structures called sclerotic rings. To scan their surroundings, owls rely on extraordinarily flexible necks containing 14 cervical vertebrae—twice as many as humans. This unique anatomy allows an owl to swivel its head up to 270 degrees in either direction without shifting its body or pinching off blood flow.

sources.title: Why Can't Owls Move Their Eyes?

cards.title: Sea sponges sneeze to purge debris without having a brain or muscles
cards.body: Despite having no brain, nerves, or muscles, sea sponges regularly perform a coordinated, full-body "sneeze." When sediment and loose debris clog the sponge's internal water-filtration canals, the animal slowly contracts its entire surface over several hours. This rhythmic squeeze secretes mucus sheets laden with trapped waste, washing out its delicate internal plumbing. It is one of the most complex behavioral responses discovered in an animal lacking a nervous system.

sources.title: Sponges Sneeze to Clean Their Pores

Their eyelids are permanently fused shut
